I never thought I’d make a post like this on LinkedIn, but I believe it’s time to make it public. A few days ago, my Microsoft offer for a Summer 2026 Software Engineering Internship was rescinded. I received an email from my recruiter stating that, since I am affected by the latest travel ban and the presidential proclamation banning (basically) all Iranians from obtaining any type of visa, my eligibility to apply for work authorization in the U.S. was automatically revoked, and therefore my offer was automatically rescinded. In my initial reply, I asked about alternative work opportunities, either remotely from Canada or from a Canadian office (since I am fully eligible to permanently live and work in Canada), but these questions were not addressed in their response, which appeared to be a general template. Something similar happened to me last year with AMD. One week before the start date of my work term, I received a phone call from AMD telling me that, since my most recent citizenship is Iranian, I could not receive an export control license to begin working. They then told me to look for alternative work opportunities one week before my start date. My original recruiter later kindly sent me a heartfelt email acknowledging the hard situation, explaining how this was outside their control. This is not a political rant, as much as I want it to be. I feel deeply hurt, and I wish all my hardworking and talented Iranian fellows, friends, and classmates peace, patience, success, and equal opportunities. I’m sharing this to try to save my career and reach out to my network to kindly ask for help. If you know of any opportunities for Summer 2026 that do not require a US-based work visa or an export license, I would truly appreciate it if you could share them with me, either in the comments so others can benefit as well, or by DM or reaching me at kiarash.sotoudeh@mail.utoronto.ca . Wishing everybody the very best and a great 2026, Kiarash

I lived in 2 worlds this summer. Well, I didn't really live in 2 worlds, but it definitely felt that way. At Wayfair , I: 🛍️ Joined the Physical Retail Sales Tech - Checkout team with Balazs Igli , Yaning Ding , Ty O'Neill , Daniel Tyson , Jiayuan Chen , and more. 🚀 Built a Dashboard for insights on Customer memberships, purchases, and browsed products for in-store assistance. The project officially went live earlier this week across 10 Wayfair Retail Stores! 🕰️ Finished my project at Week 6, and helped build a Store Search & Filter engine for all stores globally in the remaining time 💯 Learned DevOps for the first time by leveraging Kubernetes for Docker Image validation, ensuring successful deployment to Production My takeaways: ⚙️ Functional ≠ production-ready code. Most of my time at Wayfair was figuring out how to make code the most cost-efficient and maintainable. 🤝 Collaboration matters. I did not just work with engineers; I also worked with a PM, Product Designer, and field trainers. 🤩 Trust your capability. When I knew how impactful my project would be, I thought I was not ready for it. Results? I finished it 4 weeks early and expedited its official launch across all stores. In parallel, I joined a team of 4 from the Viet Tech Mentorship Program, building 0KM: A Virtual Home for Long-Distance Couples 🏠. Here's what we did: ✍ Built a digital archive of diaries for storing core relationship memories ( Thanh Dat Vu , also our tech lead) 🎵 Leveraged Spotify + YouTube for synchronized cross-device streaming ( Quinxie Doan ) 📨 Mastered SocketIo for a real-time messaging and video call feature ( Chau Tran ) 📅 Integrated Google Calendar API to surface mutual availability and enable in-app scheduling (my feature, yay!) See our full work here: https://lnkd.in/euJsr-fn To our honor, 0KM won the Technical Titan App at VTMP Day! Indeed, we could never have made it there without the support of our advisor Van Nguyen , and program leads Khoa Le Jenny Quach . What a surreal summer it has been. Looking forward to the journey lying ahead! Photo: me, Daniel Tyson (who gave me the most PR comments), Ty O'Neill (my mentor), and my project in the background #SoftwareEngineering #DevOps #FullStackDevelopment #RetailTech #Innovation #Technology #InternLife #Mentorship #Collaboration #Wayfair

Imagine you’re at home… and suddenly see your long-distance boyfriend shows up on the kiss cam 💔😔 With 0km, we can help prevent those awkward moments from happening! 4 months ago, I joined the Viet Tech Mentorship Program and teamed up with some of the coolest SWEs ever. Together, we built 0km - a full-stack React Native mobile app that helps long-distance couples stay connected through shared journals, synced Spotify sessions, YouTube streaming, chatting, and virtual date booking. My most challenging task was building the asynchronous cross-device Spotify feature that allows user to control their partner’s music. I had to think way outside the box to work around Spotify’s API limitations (it doesn’t let two users listen to the same song at once). And Supabase real-time played a huge role in helping me make it work! And that’s just part of the magic: - Thanh Dat Vu (aka our dedicated team lead) built a digital diary that lets couples share memories together (sorry Apple ’s Journal, ours is collaborative and cooler 😎) - Chau Tran wrestled with sockets to make our chat feature even smoother than Messenger. - Tuan-Anh Ngo built a matching algorithm that might just beat Google because now you can find the perfect virtual date in seconds. I didn’t expect to grow this much in just one project - not just technically, but in learning how to move fast, collaborate with top-tier teammates, and be mentored by engineers with real industry experience. We ended up winning Best Technical Execution in our Viet Tech cohort - and I’m so proud of what we built together. Massive thanks to anh Son Mac for debugging my API route for 3 hours, Anh Huy Doan for jumping into discord at 12AM right when I needed it. Our tech advisor Van Nguyen , program leads Jenny Quach and Khoa Le for guiding (and roasting) us into greatness 💪 👀 Check out our full work here: https://lnkd.in/gRtgNtZY

I’m excited to share that I’ve completed my summer internship at MaineHealth Institute for Research ! This has been one of my most memorable summers so far, and I’m incredibly honored to have had the opportunity to work under Dr. Matt Lynes on my project, “Multimodal Clustering of Post-Cardiac Arrest Syndrome (PCAS) Patients to Predict Clinical Outcome.” This summer was especially meaningful because it was my first opportunity to work with real-world human clinical data and use bioinformatics approaches. I developed a computational pipeline that integrated lipidomics data and immune cell profiles to identify distinct molecular subgroups of PCAS patients. I then used XGBoost to identify the molecular features that were most important in distinguishing these patient groups and predicting better responses to current standard treatments. Working with these two biological modalities showed me how integrating different layers of patient data can provide a more comprehensive picture of disease. More importantly, this experience gave me a new perspective on the potential of precision medicine: using patient-specific molecular information to better understand disease, predict outcomes, and potentially identify biological drivers that could inform more personalized approaches to care. Special thanks to Carolina Cora and Crystal V. for making my time in the lab so much happier, and to Dr. Andrea Tilden, Ph.D. for making all of this possible. And a huge thank you to Dr. Lynes for his mentorship and for giving me the opportunity to take on this project and grow as a researcher. I’m leaving this summer with so much gratitude, new skills, and excitement for what’s ahead! 🧬💻

If I were a freshman again, these are the extracurricular activities I’d still choose. I study Data Science & AI at Nanyang Technological University Singapore . But this year, some of my biggest shifts in thinking came from outside the classroom. Finance. Policy. Leadership. Education. Community. 1. NTU Investment Interactive Club - Singapore Financial Conference 2026 As Event Executive for SFC, Singapore's largest student-led finance conference, I ran a 500-participant event connecting students from 6 universities with professionals from firms including Goldman Sachs , BlackRock and UOB . Organizing it up close gave me a better sense of how a market conversation actually comes together: the news, the macro context in ASEAN, the people behind it. 2. Ministerial Forums - REACH Singapore × NTU-University Scholars Programme I sat in on dialogues with Singapore's leaders, including Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Minister K. Shanmugam. Coming from a technical background, these conversations forced me to think about how policy, ethics and (inter)national priorities shape the world technology gets built for. 3. NTU Honours College's programmes Being part of the founding cohort has been one of my favourite parts of university, from signature dinners to personal development programmes. What stuck with me most: the people, meeting students from completely different disciplines who think nothing as I do. Looking forward, I'm excited for our upcoming Tech-for-Good programmes, building tech and giving back to the community with people from across the cohort. 4. Code in Place - Stanford University School of Engineering My first global volunteering experience! Teaching Python fundamentals made me revisit concepts I thought I already understood. Explaining something "obvious" to someone new is a different skill entirely, and it reminded me that tech is ultimately about people, not just systems. 5. ProjectHub - Nanyang Technological University Students' Computing and Data Science Club (NTU SCDS Club) I'm currently building an AI assistant for medical translation using LLMs. Projects like this force a different kind of thinking than coursework: how do you solve a real problem, not just pass an assignment? I'm glad I didn't limit university to "things related to AI." The wider I looked, the clearer it got what I actually want to build, and why. What's one thing outside your major that has shaped how you think?
